In the late nineties in a small rural town in southern Idaho an epidemic of deaths swept through the community. All the victims were children aged five to thirteen and the prevailing theory from the local media was that it was a contagious virus like nothing that had been seen before. While this theory kept townsfolk from panicking a closer look at the phenomenon quickly dispelled the theory.

First was that only a few of the children had ever had direct contact with each other. The second was that the virus seemed to only affect boys, never girls. But the most telling of the evidence was the way the bodies were found.

Before each child died, they would all suddenly become weak and lethargic. Photos of the children showed them losing color and a few were even losing clumps of hair. The morning that each child was found dead, the bodies were all found completely drained of blood. This fact was left out of the public record.

An investigation into the deaths which would later be completely erased from public record and forgotten, with witnesses either leaving town or refusing to even mention the deaths went no where. There was no point of exit for the blood. No punctures on the body. No blood stains on the fabric or on the beds, It was as if the blood had simply disappeared.

In the fall, after thirty eight children had already been taken by the nameless cancer, the son of a home security contractor began showing symptoms. The man, whose identity has never been released was one of the minority who believed that the deaths were not accidental. He began filling his home with camera equipment and recorded everything day and night. No one was ever seen entering or leaving the home unexpectedly, but on the last day of his son’s life he noticed something strange in the recordings. The time stamp shows the time as just after four AM. His son, who’s breathing had become labored suddenly turned over in his bed. From the mattress a barely noticeable needle like object was erected where the boy’s head had been resting retracted back into the fabric.

Moments later, an object dropped from within the mattress onto the floor and quickly on eight legs scurried out from under the bed and up onto the boy. The spider, if it could be called that was at least thirty five inches in length and ten inches in height. It laid for a moment on the child’s head then quickly scurried out of sight. By the then the boy was dead.

It was days later after the funeral that the contractor had seen the boy’s killer. Quickly he took the tape to the police. Shortly after agents from various government organizations whispered into the town without being noticed. It didn’t take long before a connection was made. All of the mattresses was purchased at the same super big box store. After reviewing the store’s own security footage it was found that a single individual was shown accessing the mattresses.

Before being taken to the floor for sale, the man pulled a small container from his pocket, opened it and held the container up against the underside of the mattress for a few moments. Once he finished, he discarded of the container and moved on.

The man’s home was a secluded farm house just outside of town . When it was raided, the man was gone but his home was filled with thousands of little containers. Some were empty and some held a tiny black spider like creature which would remain motionless unless disturbed, then it would scurry quickly around the bottom of the container.

None of the large spider’s were found and once the documentation process was completed, the house was burned and the rubble was carefully collected by a hazmat team. The news reported the fire as a meth lab gone wrong but the stories of missing children stopped and were never revisited.

Euler's Disk

The commercially available toy consists of a heavy, thick chrome-plated steel disk and a rigid, slightly concave, mirrored base. Included holographic magnetic stickers can be attached to the disk, to enhance the visual effect of "sprolling" or "spolling" (spinning/rolling), but these attachments are strictly decorative. The disk, when spun on a flat surface, exhibits a spinning/rolling motion, slowly progressing through different rates and types of motion before coming to rest—most notably, the precession rate of the disk's axis of symmetry accelerates as the disk spins down. The rigid mirror is used to provide a suitable low-friction surface, with a slight concavity which keeps the spinning disk from "wandering" off a support surface.

I watched a movie the other night at a second-run theater pub, where tickets are two bucks and and craft beers are eight.

Halfway through the action flick is when the music gets slow and there are lots of close-up shots of eyes and the actors start talking about feelings. And wheezing. It takes me a minute to realize the wheezing isn't part of the movie. I start to wonder if the sound is broken when I notice people in the rows in front of me start looking around.

I finally look across the aisle, squinting into the darkness and this mammoth sized ball of mayonnaise completely absorbing the seat. It's impossible to tell the gender. For the next hour this shrill wheezing penetrates the theater. Across the aisle where I'm sitting, at least 5 seats deep and 3 rows down, people continued to swivel their heads looking for the source of this jet plane.
The wheezing of a jet plane
Gosh that must've been annoying. People get angry at cell phones ringing so a constant wheezing - man that would've ruined the movie theater experience for me.

"The Hitchhikers Guide to the Galaxy" is the ultimate space opera IMHO. But only the first two books are worth reading, the other three are lame.

• Saturn's Children by Charles Stross
  • Implied Spaces by Walter Jon Williams

Neither of these books is hard sci-fi. They're like sci-fi beach reads and they're both fun reads. I highly recommend both of them.

I would like to second Saturn's Child, and add to it Neptune's Brood, by the same author. It is set in the same universe, but much farther in the future. An android, who is an expert on confidence games (cons and scams) for her family's bank hitches a ride on a church/rocketship that is trying to resurrect the human race; she is trying to reunite with her sister, who may have solved an old mystery, making them both rich and hunted. Very interesting read.
Iain M Bank's Culture Series A great selection of stories in a world that really feels like it lives and breathes.
After you have tried all the others, why not try 'The Mote in Gods eye' by Larry Niven. It's about first contact and really does a good job of it.

John Scalzi is sort of a dweeb, but his Old Man's War books are enjoyable.

Mandatory reading: The Forever War by Joe Haldeman. Ditto on Dune and Ender's Game.

A fun read for me was Down and Out in the Magic Kingdom, by Cory Doctorow. It tells about a man working with a group to run Disneyworld in a post-scarcity economy, where your value is determined by how much your contributions to society are appreciated by others. With cloning and downloading your mind, everyone is effectively immortal, with it being so commonplace that some people upload to a new body just to get over a cold.
